blocks.html: In Dimensional Analysis you used units to convert from one unit to another, letting the units you didn't want cancel. Physics uses the same habit for a second job: checking equations. Before you trust a formula, or an answer, look at its units.
Units multiply, divide and cancel just like algebra. Every term that is added, subtracted or set equal in an equation must have the same units. If they don't match, the equation is wrong.

An equation says two amounts are the same quantity. A length can equal a length, but it can never equal a time, just as 3 meters can't be "the same as" 3 seconds. Adding works the same way: $3\ \text{m} + 2\ \text{s}$ has no meaning, so any formula that asks you to do it must be misremembered.

blocks.title: Checking a motion equation
blocks.q: Check the units of $x = v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2$.
steps: Left side: $x$ is a position, in m.
Second term: $\tfrac12$ has no units, so $a t^2$ has units $\dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2} \cdot \text{s}^2 = \text{m}$.
Every term is in meters, so the equation passes the test.
blocks.a: The units match: m = m + m.

blocks.title: Catching a slip
blocks.q: A student remembers the speed of a falling object as $v = 2gh$. Is that possible?
steps: A speed is in $\dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}$, so the two sides don't match.
Taking a square root fixes the units: $\sqrt{\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2} = \text{m/s}$. The real formula is $v = \sqrt{2gh}$.

blocks.title: Units of an answer
blocks.q: You compute $\dfrac{v^2}{a}$ with $v$ in m/s and $a$ in m/s². What kind of quantity did you find?
blocks.a: A length, in meters (it shows up later as a stopping distance).

blocks.html: Adding quantities with different units, or keeping an answer whose units don't fit the question. If you are asked for a distance and your answer comes out in m/s, you used the wrong formula or dropped a factor of time. Quick check: write the units next to every number as you work, and look at the units of the final answer before you look at its size.
Matching units can't catch a missing $\tfrac12$ or a wrong factor of 2, because plain numbers have no units. Units prove an equation wrong; they can't prove it right.

blocks.html: In Distance and Displacement you met the difference between how far you went and where you ended up. To work with numbers, physicists put the motion on an axis: pick an origin ($x = 0$) and a positive direction. Then every position is a signed number, like the integers in Subtracting Integers.

Displacement is final position minus initial position: $\Delta x = x_f - x_i$. Its sign tells the direction: positive means it ended up on the $+x$ side of where it started, negative means the $-x$ side.

Subtraction measures the gap between two numbers on a number line, including which way you step to get from the first to the second. Going from $x = 2$ to $x = 7$ is a step of $+5$; going from $7$ back to $2$ is a step of $-5$. Displacement is exactly that step, for the whole trip at once, so it ignores everything that happened in between.

blocks.html: Velocity: Speed with a Direction is speed with a direction. With positions on an axis, we can make that exact. Over a time interval $\Delta t$, divide the displacement by the time.
Average velocity: $v_{avg} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$, with a sign. Average speed: $\dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\Delta t}$, never negative.

The average velocity is the one steady velocity that would carry you from the same start to the same end in the same time. That is why only the displacement matters: a steady motion can't turn around, so it only "sees" where you began and where you finished. Average speed answers a different question: how fast, on average, you covered ground.

steps: $v_{avg} = \dfrac{-12\ \text{m}}{4\ \text{s}} = -3\ \text{m/s}$, so it moved in the $-x$ direction at 3 m/s on average.

steps: Distance: $40 + 10 = 50\ \text{m}$, so the average speed is $\dfrac{50}{40} = 1.25\ \text{m/s}$.

blocks.title: The averaging trap
blocks.q: You drive $60\ \text{km}$ at $30\ \text{km/h}$, then $60\ \text{km}$ at $60\ \text{km/h}$. What is your average speed?
steps: Not $45\ \text{km/h}$: you spent twice as long at the slow speed, so it counts twice as much.

blocks.html: Averaging the starting and ending speeds, or the speeds of the legs, as if each counted equally. That only works when each speed lasts the same amount of time (or when the velocity changes at a steady rate). Safe method: always go back to the definition, total displacement (or distance) divided by total time.

blocks.html: A position-time ($x$–$t$) graph plots where an object is at each moment. Its most useful feature is its slope, which you can find with The Slope Formula. Over any straight piece, rise over run is $\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$, which is exactly the Average Velocity.
The slope of an $x$–$t$ graph is the velocity. Steeper means faster; upward slope means moving in the $+x$ direction; downward slope means $-x$; flat means standing still.

The rise of the graph is a change in position, $\Delta x$, and the run is a change in time, $\Delta t$. Dividing gives $\Delta x / \Delta t$, the definition of velocity. The height of the graph only tells you where the object is, not how fast it moves.

blocks.html: A speedometer shows your velocity right now, not over a trip. On a curved position-time graph the slope keeps changing, so we need the slope at a single point.
The instantaneous velocity at time $t$ is the slope of the tangent line to the $x$–$t$ graph at $t$: the line that just touches the curve there and runs in the same direction.

Take the average velocity over a short interval around $t$, then a shorter one, then shorter still. On a smooth curve, zooming in makes the curve look straighter and straighter, and those average-velocity lines settle down to one line: the tangent. Its slope is the velocity at that instant. In calculus this is the derivative, but the idea only needs slopes.

blocks.html: In Acceleration acceleration was how quickly velocity changes. Now velocities carry signs, so acceleration does too, and its sign holds a surprise.

$a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{v_f - v_i}{\Delta t}$. An object speeds up when $a$ and $v$ point the same way and slows down when they point opposite ways. The sign of $a$ alone doesn't tell you which.

Acceleration points in the direction of the change in velocity. A car moving in the $-x$ direction at $-10\ \text{m/s}$ that speeds up to $-16\ \text{m/s}$ has a change of $-6\ \text{m/s}$: its acceleration is negative and it is speeding up. "Negative" is a direction on your axis, not a word for "slowing".

blocks.html: A velocity-time ($v$–$t$) graph looks like the x–t graphs you know, but it answers different questions. Its height is the velocity, and two features carry the rest of the story: its slope and the area under it.
On a $v$–$t$ graph, the slope is the Acceleration and Its Sign and the area between the graph and the time axis is the displacement (area below the axis counts as negative).

Slope: rise over run is $\Delta v / \Delta t$, which is the definition of acceleration. Area: at a steady velocity, displacement is $v \times \Delta t$, which is the area of a rectangle of height $v$ and width $\Delta t$. When $v$ changes, slice the time into thin strips; each strip is nearly a rectangle, so adding the strips adds up the little displacements. Shapes from Area of a Trapezoid do the adding for you when the pieces are straight.

blocks.html: You can now read slopes on an x–t graph and slopes and areas on a v–t graph. Put those together and any one motion graph lets you sketch the other two. This is one of the most useful skills in mechanics, and one of the most often missed.
Going down the chain $x \to v \to a$, take slopes: the value of each graph is the slope of the one above it. Going up $a \to v \to x$, add up areas, starting from the known initial value.

Velocity is the rate of change of position, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. A rate of change is a slope. Undoing a slope means adding up small changes, and adding up a rate times small time steps is an area. So the three graphs are linked by the same two moves every time.

blocks.html: When the acceleration is constant, the v–t graph is a straight line. That one fact gives the two main equations of motion, and you can read both straight off the graph.
For constant acceleration: $v = v_0 + at$ and $x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2$. They hold only while the acceleration stays the same.

A straight $v$–$t$ line starting at $v_0$ with slope $a$ has height $v_0 + at$ at time $t$: that is the first equation. The displacement is the area under that line, which splits into a rectangle ($v_0 \times t$) and a triangle on top ($\tfrac12 \times t \times at$). Adding them gives $\Delta x = v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2$, the second equation.

blocks.html: Sometimes the time is neither given nor wanted: a car's braking distance, a jet's runway length. You could find $t$ first from the constant-acceleration equations, but one more equation skips that step.
$v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$ links the speeds and the displacement without the time. It also needs constant acceleration.

Start from the area under the straight $v$–$t$ line: a trapezoid, $\Delta x = \tfrac12(v_0 + v)\,t$. The first equation gives $t = \dfrac{v - v_0}{a}$. Substitute: $$\Delta x = \dfrac{(v + v_0)(v - v_0)}{2a} = \dfrac{v^2 - v_0^2}{2a}.$$ Multiply both sides by $2a$ and the time is gone: $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$.

blocks.html: Drop anything and, if air resistance is small, it falls with the same constant acceleration. From Mass and Weight, the gravitational force on a mass $m$ is $mg$; Newton's second law gives its acceleration as that force divided by the same mass.
In free fall every object accelerates downward at $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, whatever its mass. With up as positive, $a = -9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, and the constant-acceleration equations apply.

A heavier object is pulled harder, but it also has more inertia to overcome, in exactly the same proportion: $a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{mg}{m} = g$. The mass cancels. In 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the airless Moon, and they landed together.

blocks.html: Throw a ball straight up and it is in Free Fall the moment it leaves your hand: on the way up, at the top and on the way down. One acceleration, $9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ downward, covers the whole flight, so one set of equations does too.
With up positive, $a = -9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ for the entire flight. At the top, $v = 0$ for an instant, but the acceleration is still $9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ downward.

Gravity doesn't switch off at the top. The velocity is changing there from up to down, and a changing velocity means an acceleration. If $a$ really were zero at the top, the ball would hover there forever. The flight is also symmetric: going up loses $9.8\ \text{m/s}$ each second and coming down gains it back, so the trip up and the trip down take equal times and the ball returns to your hand at its launch speed.

blocks.html: Displacement, velocity, acceleration and force all have a size and a direction: they are vectors. In two dimensions the easiest way to handle a vector is to split it into an $x$-part and a $y$-part, using the Sine, Cosine and Tangent you know from geometry.

A vector of magnitude $A$ at angle $\theta$ from the $+x$ axis has components $A_x = A\cos\theta$ and $A_y = A\sin\theta$. In general: the component along the side adjacent to the angle uses cosine; the one opposite uses sine.

Draw the vector as the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs lie along the axes. The legs are the components. Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, so the adjacent leg is $A\cos\theta$; sine is opposite over hypotenuse, so the opposite leg is $A\sin\theta$. Which leg is "adjacent" depends on which axis the angle is measured from, not on whether it is $x$ or $y$.

blocks.html: Using sine for the $x$-component every time (or cosine every time). It depends on where the angle is measured from. Quick checks: as $\theta \to 0$ from an axis, the component along that axis should approach the whole vector (cosine does that). And the two components must satisfy $A_x^2 + A_y^2 = A^2$.

blocks.html: Two pushes on a box, two legs of a trip, a boat's velocity plus a river's current: vectors keep needing to be added. Arrows can't simply be added like numbers, because directions matter. Splitting each into components turns the problem back into ordinary arithmetic.

To add vectors, add their $x$-components and add their $y$-components: $R_x = A_x + B_x$, $R_y = A_y + B_y$. Then $R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2}$, and its direction comes from $\tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)$, checked against the quadrant.

Placing the arrows head to tail, the total east-west movement is the sum of each arrow's east-west part, and likewise north-south; the directions along one axis don't interfere with the other. Rebuilding the resultant from its two perpendicular parts is a right triangle again, so the Pythagorean theorem gives its size and inverse tangent gives its angle.

blocks.html: A velocity is always measured relative to something. Walking at $1.5\ \text{m/s}$ on a moving walkway, you move faster relative to the floor than relative to the walkway. When frames move relative to each other, velocities combine by Adding Vectors by Components.

$$\vec{v}_{\text{object, ground}} = \vec{v}_{\text{object, medium}} + \vec{v}_{\text{medium, ground}}.$$ For a boat: its velocity relative to the shore is its velocity relative to the water plus the water's velocity relative to the shore.

In one second, the water carries the boat some distance downstream while the boat moves through the water in the direction it points. Its total displacement relative to the shore is the sum of the two, so its velocity is too. Because the two motions add as vectors, a current at right angles to the boat's heading doesn't help or hinder the crossing; it only moves the boat sideways.

blocks.html: Roll a marble off a table. While it flies, gravity pulls it down exactly as in Free Fall, and nothing pushes it sideways. Treat the two components of its motion separately, and the problem splits into two easy ones that share the same clock.

For a horizontal launch from height $h$: horizontally, $v_x$ stays constant; vertically, it falls from rest with $a = -9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$. The time in the air, $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$, depends only on the height.

Forces change motion only along their own direction. Gravity is vertical, so it changes $v_y$ and leaves $v_x$ alone. With no air resistance, the horizontal motion is steady and the vertical motion is a drop from rest, so a ball launched sideways and a ball dropped at the same moment from the same height hit the floor together.

blocks.html: A kicked ball, a thrown javelin, a stone from a catapult: each starts with a velocity at an angle. Split it into components, and you have a vertical launch and a steady horizontal motion running side by side, exactly as for a horizontal launch.

Launch at speed $v_0$ and angle $\theta$: $v_{0x} = v_0\cos\theta$ stays the same all flight; $v_{0y} = v_0\sin\theta$ changes by $-9.8\ \text{m/s}$ each second. On level ground the path is symmetric: up time equals down time.

Only gravity acts during the flight, and it is vertical. So the vertical motion is a throw straight up with speed $v_{0y}$, and the horizontal motion is steady at $v_{0x}$. At the top only $v_y$ is zero; the ball still moves sideways at $v_{0x}$. For level ground the range is $v_{0x} \times \dfrac{2v_{0y}}{g} = \dfrac{2v_0^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g}$, which is the same for $\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$.

blocks.html: Newton's Second Law: F = ma relates the net force on an object to its acceleration. But what counts as "the object"? A car with passengers, two carts tied together, a whole train? In physics you get to choose: the things you include form the system, and everything else is the surroundings.

Forces between parts of the system are internal; forces from outside are external. Only external forces change the motion of the system's center of mass, the mass-weighted average position: $x_{cm} = \dfrac{m_1x_1 + m_2x_2 + \cdots}{m_1 + m_2 + \cdots}$.

Internal forces come in third-law pairs, equal and opposite, both inside the system, so they cancel when you add up all the forces on the system. What's left is the external force, and it moves the system as if all the mass sat at one point. That point is a weighted mean: like a fair share, but heavier parts get more say.

blocks.html: You've met forces in Newton's Third Law and Friction. Before using Newton's laws on any problem, physicists draw a free-body diagram: one object, alone, with every force on it drawn as an arrow.

Draw the object as a box or a dot. For every force on it, draw an arrow from its center in the force's direction and name the object that exerts it. Contact forces come from things touching it; gravity comes from Earth.

Newton's laws relate the forces on one object to that object's motion. A diagram that leaves out a force, or adds one that isn't real, gives the wrong net force. Naming who exerts each force is the test: "the floor pushes up" is a real force; "the motion pushes forward" has no one doing the pushing, so it isn't a force.

blocks.html: Newton's Third Law said forces come in pairs. With Free-Body Diagrams we can say exactly which forces pair up, and it is not always the pair you expect.

If A exerts a force on B, then B exerts a force on A that is equal in size, opposite in direction and of the same type. The two forces act on different objects, so they never appear on the same free-body diagram.

A force is an interaction between two objects, and an interaction has two ends. When your hand pushes a wall, the wall pushes your hand: one interaction, seen from each side. Because the forces act on different objects, they can't cancel each other; each changes the motion of its own object according to that object's mass.

blocks.html: Newton's First Law: Inertia said an object keeps its velocity unless a net force acts. With Free-Body Diagrams, that becomes a tool: whenever the velocity is constant, the forces on the diagram must add to zero.

Equilibrium means $\Sigma \vec{F} = 0$, which happens exactly when the velocity is constant: at rest, or moving in a straight line at a steady speed. In components: $\Sigma F_x = 0$ and $\Sigma F_y = 0$.

A net force changes velocity; that is what the second law says. So if the velocity isn't changing, there is no net force, whatever the speed. A car cruising at $30\ \text{m/s}$ on a straight road is in equilibrium just as much as a parked car: the forward force from the road exactly balances drag and rolling friction.

blocks.html: Newton's Second Law: F = ma gave $F = ma$. When several forces act, which $F$? The answer is the net force, the sum of all the forces on your free-body diagram, with signs. When that sum is zero, there is no acceleration.
$\Sigma F_x = ma_x$: choose a positive direction, add every force along that axis with its sign, then divide by the mass.

Each force on an object contributes to its acceleration, and forces along a line simply add, with opposite directions subtracting. The object responds to the total, so only the net force sets the acceleration. A large push opposed by large friction can give a small acceleration.

blocks.html: A floor pushes up on whatever rests on it. That push, perpendicular to the surface, is the normal force $F_N$. With the second law along an axis you can find it in any situation, and it is often not $mg$.
The normal force is whatever size the surface must push to keep the object from moving into it. Find it from $\Sigma F_y = ma_y$. A bathroom scale reads the normal force, your apparent weight.

A surface is like a very stiff spring: pressed harder, it squeezes slightly more and pushes back harder. It has no fixed value. Stand still and it balances gravity. Ride an elevator that accelerates upward, and the floor must push harder than $mg$ to speed you up; accelerate downward, and it pushes less.

blocks.html: Ropes pull at angles, handles push at angles. A force at an angle acts partly along each axis, so you split it with components and use the second law along each axis separately.

The $x$ and $y$ directions are independent, as they were for adding vectors: the horizontal part of a pull can only change horizontal motion, and its vertical part only vertical motion. blocks.html: On a ramp, the motion runs along the slope, so the smart choice of axes tilts with it: $x$ along the slope, $y$ perpendicular to it. The normal force then lies along $y$, and only gravity needs to be split into components.

On a ramp at angle $\theta$, gravity splits into $mg\sin\theta$ along the slope (downhill) and $mg\cos\theta$ into the slope. Without friction, $F_N = mg\cos\theta$ and $a = g\sin\theta$ down the slope.

The angle between the weight (straight down) and the perpendicular to the ramp equals the ramp angle $\theta$, because both lines are turned by the same amount from the vertical and the ramp from the horizontal. So the into-the-slope part is adjacent to $\theta$ (cosine) and the along-the-slope part is opposite (sine). Check the extremes: on flat ground ($\theta = 0$), nothing pulls along the surface; on a vertical wall ($\theta = 90^\circ$), all of gravity is along it.

blocks.html: When one surface slides over another, friction acts against the sliding. For many pairs of dry surfaces, its size follows a simple rule that depends on the The Normal Force and Apparent Weight.

Kinetic friction: $f_k = \mu_k F_N$, directed opposite to the sliding. The coefficient $\mu_k$ (no units) depends on the two surfaces; typical values run from about $0.03$ (oiled steel on steel) to about $0.7$ (rubber on dry concrete).

Surfaces touch only at tiny bumps. Pressing them together harder flattens the bumps into more contact, and the extra contact resists sliding in proportion. So friction grows with how hard the surfaces press, which is the normal force, not the weight. For a box on level ground those are equal; on a ramp, with an extra push or with a slanted pull, they are not.

blocks.html: Push gently on a heavy dresser and it doesn't move. Something matches your push exactly: static friction, the grip between surfaces that aren't sliding. Unlike Kinetic Friction, it has no fixed size.

Static friction is as large as it needs to be to prevent sliding, up to a limit: $f_s \le \mu_s F_N$. Below the limit, find $f_s$ from the balance of forces; past the limit, the object starts to slide and kinetic friction takes over.

At rest, the net force is zero, so friction must cancel whatever else pushes along the surface. Push with $50\ \text{N}$ and friction gives $50\ \text{N}$; push with $80\ \text{N}$ and it gives $80\ \text{N}$, until the bumps between the surfaces can't hold any more. Usually $\mu_s > \mu_k$, which is why a stuck object lurches once it breaks free.

blocks.html: Put together Inclined Planes and Static Friction, and a ramp becomes a friction meter. Tilt a board slowly with a block on it: at first static friction holds it, then at one particular angle it lets go.

A block starts to slip when $\tan\theta = \mu_s$. Once sliding down, kinetic friction points up the slope: $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$. Sliding up, both gravity's part and friction point down the slope: the deceleration is $g(\sin\theta + \mu_k\cos\theta)$.

Along the slope, gravity pulls with $mg\sin\theta$; static friction can resist with at most $\mu_s F_N = \mu_s mg\cos\theta$. The block holds while $mg\sin\theta \le \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, that is, while $\tan\theta \le \mu_s$. The mass cancels, so a heavy block and a light one of the same material slip at the same angle. Friction always opposes sliding (or the sliding that would happen), so its direction flips when the motion does.

blocks.html: Trains of carts, a block pulled by a hanging weight, two boxes pushed together: the objects move together, so they share one acceleration. The trick is choosing the right system for each question, then using Newton's Second Law Along an Axis.

To find the shared acceleration, treat all the linked objects as one system: the forces between them are internal and cancel. To find a rope tension or a contact force, take one object alone: then that force is external and appears in its equation.

Each choice of system leaves out different forces. The whole train hides the ropes between the cars, so its equation has only the outside pull and the total mass. A single car shows its rope as an ordinary force. Both equations are true at once, and using them in that order gives each unknown with the least algebra.

blocks.html: A string over a pulley turns one object's downward pull into another's upward or sideways motion. The classic example, the Atwood machine, is two masses hanging on either side of a pulley. It is a connected-objects problem with a bend in the string.

A light string over a light, frictionless pulley has the same tension everywhere. Measure each object's acceleration along the string: the objects share one acceleration $a$. For an Atwood machine, $a = \dfrac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2}$ and the tension lies between the two weights.

Treat the whole string as a bent axis. Along it, the heavier block's weight drives the system forward and the lighter block's weight holds it back, while the tension pulls equally on both ends and cancels as an internal force. So the net driving force is $(m_2 - m_1)g$, shared by the total mass. Then either block alone gives the tension.

blocks.html: Stretch a spring and it pulls back; squeeze it and it pushes back. For most springs, as long as you don't overstretch them, the force is proportional to how far you deform them.

Hooke's law: $F = kx$, where $x$ is the stretch or compression from the spring's natural (relaxed) length and $k$ is the spring constant in N/m. The spring's force points back toward the natural length.

A spring is a long coil of metal, and each little piece of the wire twists slightly when you stretch it. Twice the stretch twists each piece twice as much, and the metal pushes back twice as hard. So the force grows in proportion, and $k$ tells how stiff the spring is: the newtons needed for each meter of stretch.

blocks.html: Gravity: Mass and Distance described gravity in words: more mass, more pull; more distance, less pull. Newton made it exact, and the same law describes a falling apple and the Moon's orbit.

Every two masses attract each other with $F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$, where $r$ is the distance between their centers and $G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$. Each object feels the same size force (a third-law pair).

The pull grows with each mass, so it is proportional to the product $m_1m_2$. It spreads out in all directions from a mass, over spheres whose areas grow as $r^2$, so it weakens as $1/r^2$: twice as far, a quarter of the pull. Newton showed that a uniform sphere pulls on things outside it as if all its mass were at its center, which is why $r$ is measured center to center.

blocks.html: Instead of computing Newton's Law of Gravitation for every object, describe what a planet does to the space around it: the force on each kilogram placed there. That is the gravitational field strength, and near Earth's surface you already know its value.
$g = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{GM}{r^2}$, in N/kg, which is the same as m/s². At Earth's surface it is $9.8\ \text{N/kg}$; it shrinks with distance from Earth's center but never reaches zero.

Divide Newton's law by the small mass: $\dfrac{GMm/r^2}{m} = \dfrac{GM}{r^2}$. What's left depends only on the planet and the distance, not on the object. And by the second law, an object in free fall accelerates at $F/m$, which is $g$. So the field strength and the free-fall acceleration are the same number.

blocks.html: Velocity is a vector, so it can change in two ways: in size or in direction. Acceleration and Its Sign includes both. A car rounding a curve at a steady speed is accelerating, because its direction keeps turning.
An object moving at steady speed $v$ around a circle of radius $r$ accelerates toward the center with $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$.

Take the velocity at two nearby moments and subtract them as vectors: the change points toward the center of the circle. How big is it? In time $\Delta t$ the velocity turns through the same angle as the radius, $\Delta\theta = v\Delta t/r$, so the change has size about $v\,\Delta\theta = v^2\Delta t/r$. Divide by $\Delta t$: $a = v^2/r$. Faster means the velocity is both bigger and turning sooner, which is why $v$ is squared.

blocks.html: If an object has Centripetal Acceleration, the second law says a net force must point toward the center too. That force isn't a new kind of force. Some real push or pull, one you can name, does the job.
For motion in a circle, the net inward force is $\Sigma F_{in} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. Tension, friction, gravity or a normal force supplies it. Nothing pushes outward.

Without an inward force, an object moves in a straight line (the first law). The inward force keeps bending its path. On a flat road, the only horizontal force on a car is static friction from the road, so friction must supply all of $mv^2/r$; that sets a top speed, $v = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$. For the Moon, Earth's gravity does the job; for a ball on a string, the tension does.

blocks.html: Roller coasters, dips in the road, a bucket swung overhead: here the circle stands upright, and gravity takes part. At the top and bottom of the circle, gravity and the other force line up with the center, so Forces in Circular Motion works along one vertical axis.

At the top or bottom, take "toward the center" as positive and write $\Sigma F_{toward} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. At the bottom of a dip, $F_N = m\left(g + \dfrac{v^2}{r}\right)$; at the top of a hill, $F_N = m\left(g - \dfrac{v^2}{r}\right)$.

At the bottom of a dip the center is above you, so the net force must point up: the seat pushes up harder than gravity pulls down, and you feel heavier. Over the top of a hill the center is below, so the net force points down: the seat pushes up less than gravity, and you feel lighter. If $v^2/r$ reaches $g$, the seat pushes nothing at all and you lift off. At the top of a loop, both gravity and the track push toward the center, so the smallest speed that keeps contact is $v = \sqrt{gr}$.

blocks.html: In Work work was force times distance. That holds when the force points along the motion. When it points at an angle, only part of it, its component along the motion, does work.

The work done by a constant force is $W = Fd\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Work is in joules ($1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$) and can be positive, negative or zero.

Work measures how much a force adds to (or takes from) an object's energy of motion. A force helps the motion only through its part along the motion, $F\cos\theta$. If the force points backward ($\theta = 180^\circ$, like friction), it takes energy away: negative work. If it is perpendicular ($\theta = 90^\circ$), it neither helps nor hinders: zero work, however hard it pushes.

blocks.html: $W = Fd$ needs one steady force. A spring's force grows as you stretch it, and a rocket's thrust changes as it climbs. A graph of force against position handles any of them, the same way the area under a v–t graph gave displacement.
The work done by a force along a straight path is the area under its force-position ($F$–$x$) graph, counted negative where the force is negative.

Slice the path into short steps. Over each step the force is nearly constant, so the work there is $F\,\Delta x$: the area of a thin strip. Adding up all the strips adds up the work. For a force that changes, using the final force times the whole distance counts the big end value over the whole path and overestimates the work.

blocks.html: Kinetic Energy is $K = \tfrac12 mv^2$. Work by a Constant Force says how much a force adds or removes. Put them together and you get one of the most useful shortcuts in mechanics.

The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: $W_{net} = \Delta K = \tfrac12 mv_f^2 - \tfrac12 mv_i^2$. $W_{net}$ is the sum of the work done by every force, which equals the work done by the net force.

For a constant net force along the motion, $W_{net} = F_{net}\,d = ma\,d$. From motion without the time, $a\,d = \tfrac12(v_f^2 - v_i^2)$. Multiply by $m$: $W_{net} = \tfrac12 mv_f^2 - \tfrac12 mv_i^2$. So kinetic energy is exactly the quantity that the net work changes, and the theorem holds for changing forces too (add up the work in small steps).

blocks.html: In Gravitational Potential Energy you met $PE = mgh$. Now look closely at where that energy lives. It isn't stored in the lifted book alone; it belongs to the book and Earth together, because it depends on how far apart they are.

For an object–Earth system near Earth's surface, $\Delta U_g = mg\,\Delta h$. Only changes in $U_g$ matter, so you may put $U_g = 0$ at any convenient height. $\Delta U_g$ depends only on the change in height, not on the path.

Lift a book at steady speed and you do work $mg\,\Delta h$ against gravity, but the book's kinetic energy doesn't change. The energy went into the separation between the book and Earth. Gravity's work on any path depends only on how far up or down you end, because only the vertical parts of the path count. So the stored energy is path-independent, and that is what makes it a potential energy.

blocks.html: A stretched spring can launch a toy or start a clock, so it stores energy. How much? It equals the work done to deform it, which is the area under the force-stretch graph.
A spring stretched or compressed by $x$ from its natural length stores elastic potential energy $U_s = \tfrac12 kx^2$.

The force needed grows from $0$ to $kx$ as you stretch the spring (Hooke's law), so the $F$–$x$ graph is a straight line through the origin. The work is the triangle under it: $\tfrac12 \times x \times kx = \tfrac12 kx^2$. The $\tfrac12$ comes from the triangle; the square comes from the force and the distance both growing with $x$.

blocks.html: The work-energy theorem counts the work of every force. Gravity's work and a spring's work can be tracked instead as changes in gravitational and elastic potential energy. If nothing else does work, the total stays fixed.
When only gravity and springs do work, the mechanical energy is conserved: $K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$, with $U = U_g + U_s$.

Gravity's work on the object is $-\Delta U_g$ and the spring's is $-\Delta U_s$. If they are the only forces doing work, the work-energy theorem gives $-\Delta U_g - \Delta U_s = \Delta K$, so $\Delta K + \Delta U = 0$. Normal forces on a frictionless track and the tension in a pendulum string are perpendicular to the motion, so they do no work and don't spoil this.

blocks.html: Conservation of Mechanical Energy is easiest to use as bookkeeping. An energy bar chart shows the energy at the start, the energy that crosses the boundary of your system, and the energy at the end, as bars you can count.

Choose the system. Then: energy at the start $+$ work done by outside forces $=$ energy at the end, where the energies are $K$, $U_g$, $U_s$ and thermal energy $E_{th}$. The bars on the left plus the work must equal the bars on the right.

Energy can change form inside the system and can cross its boundary as work, but it is never created or destroyed. So the total before, plus whatever enters as work (minus whatever leaves), must equal the total after. Choosing the system decides which forces count as "outside": with Earth inside the system, gravity shows up as $U_g$; with Earth outside, it shows up as work instead. Either way works, as long as you don't count it twice.

blocks.html: Push a box across the floor and let go: it slows and stops. Its kinetic energy is gone, but energy is conserved. It turned into thermal energy, warming both the box and the floor, by an amount you can calculate with Kinetic Friction.

When kinetic friction $f_k$ acts while two surfaces slide a distance $d$ past each other, it turns mechanical energy into thermal energy: $\Delta E_{th} = f_k d$. Then $K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f + \Delta E_{th}$.

Friction comes from countless tiny bumps snagging and letting go, which sets the atoms near both surfaces jiggling faster. Faster random jiggling is higher temperature. The energy isn't destroyed; it changes from the ordered motion of the whole box into the disordered motion of its atoms and the floor's. That's why rubbing your hands together warms them.

blocks.html: Power measured how fast energy is transferred. Two students climbing the same stairs do the same Work by a Constant Force, but the one who runs delivers it faster.
Power is the rate of energy transfer: $P = \dfrac{W}{\Delta t}$, in watts ($1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J/s}$). For a force pushing along the velocity, $P = Fv$.

Work divided by time is a rate, like speed is distance divided by time. If a force $F$ pushes along the motion, in a short time $\Delta t$ the object moves $v\Delta t$, so the work is $Fv\Delta t$ and the power is $Fv$. That's why a car's engine works hardest at highway speed: drag is large and so is $v$.

blocks.html: $mgh$ assumes the field $g$ stays the same. For rockets and satellites it doesn't: $g$ weakens with distance from Earth's center. Adding up the work against the full law of gravitation gives a formula that works at any distance, and it comes with a minus sign.
For two masses a distance $r$ apart (center to center), $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, choosing $U = 0$ when they are infinitely far apart. $U$ rises toward zero as they separate.

Pulling the masses apart takes positive work, because gravity pulls them together, and that work raises $U$. Going outward, the force weakens as $1/r^2$, and the area under the force-distance graph from $r$ out to infinity is finite: $\dfrac{GMm}{r}$. Since $U$ must rise by that much to reach $0$ at infinity, it starts at $-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$. Near the surface, the change between $R$ and $R + h$ is very close to $mgh$.

blocks.html: In Physical Science you met momentum as mass times velocity. Physics 1 adds one important idea: momentum is a vector. It points the way the object moves, so on a line it carries a sign, and in a plane it has components, just like the vectors you add by components.

Momentum is $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$, measured in $\text{kg·m/s}$. On a line, pick a positive direction and give each momentum a sign. The momentum of a system is the vector sum of the momenta of its parts: $\vec{p}_{\text{tot}} = m_1\vec{v}_1 + m_2\vec{v}_2 + \dots$

Why multiply mass by velocity? Because that product is what a force changes. Newton's second law says $F = ma = m\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$, so $F\Delta t = \Delta(mv)$: a push lasting a while changes $mv$, whatever the mass. A loaded truck and a bicycle at the same speed are very different to stop, and $mv$ measures exactly that difference. Since velocity has a direction, so does $mv$, and two momenta in opposite directions cancel when you add them.

blocks.html: You know from Newton's second law that a net force changes velocity, and from Softening a Collision that stretching a collision over more time softens it. Impulse puts those two ideas into one equation.

Start from $\Sigma F = ma$ and write the acceleration as $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$. Multiply both sides by $\Delta t$: $$\Sigma F\,\Delta t = m\Delta v = \Delta p.$$ The left side, force times the time it acts, is called the impulse $J$. A big force for a short time and a small force for a long time can give the same impulse, and so the same change in momentum.

Impulse equals change in momentum: $J = F_{\text{avg}}\Delta t = \Delta p = m v_f - m v_i$. Its unit, $\text{N·s}$, is the same as $\text{kg·m/s}$. When the force changes during the push, the impulse is the area under the force–time graph.

blocks.html: An impulse changes an object's momentum. But in a collision every push comes in a pair, by Newton's third law, and that pairing makes the total momentum of the two objects stay fixed.

During a collision, A pushes B with force $\vec{F}$ and B pushes A with $-\vec{F}$, for exactly the same time $\Delta t$ (they touch for as long as they touch). So $$\Delta\vec{p}_B = \vec{F}\Delta t, \qquad \Delta\vec{p}_A = -\vec{F}\Delta t.$$ Add them: $\Delta\vec{p}_A + \Delta\vec{p}_B = 0$. Whatever momentum A loses, B gains. Nothing in that argument cares whether the objects bounce, stick or crumple.

If the net outside force on a system is zero (or its impulse is negligible during a short collision), the total momentum stays the same: $$m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = m_1 v_1' + m_2 v_2'.$$ Forces between parts of the system are internal and cancel in pairs.

Check outside forces. On a level frictionless track, gravity and the normal force cancel. Friction from the road is outside, but during a quick crash its impulse is small.

blocks.html: When two objects stick together, momentum conservation alone tells you everything: after the collision there is only one velocity to find.

For objects that stick: $$m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = (m_1 + m_2)\,v.$$ This is a perfectly inelastic collision. Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not: the most kinetic energy that momentum allows turns into thermal energy, sound and bent material.

Why must kinetic energy be lost? Take a cart hitting an identical cart at rest. Momentum forces the pair to move at $v/2$. Kinetic energy before: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. After: $\tfrac{1}{2}(2m)(v/2)^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}mv^2$. Half of it is gone. In general, when a moving $m_1$ sticks to a resting $m_2$, the fraction lost is $\dfrac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$. The energy hasn't vanished; it went into the Velcro, the putty or the crumpled bumper as heat and sound.

blocks.html: Sticking collisions are useful for measuring speeds that are hard to time. Fire a dart into a block on ice, measure how fast the block slides off, and momentum gives the dart's speed: $v = \dfrac{(m + M)V}{m}$. The heavier the block, the slower and easier to measure its motion.

blocks.html: In every collision momentum is conserved. Kinetic energy is a different story, and comparing it before and after is how physicists sort collisions into kinds.

Momentum
Kinetic energy
Example

blocks.cap: Momentum is conserved in all three. Kinetic energy decides the label.

blocks.html: To classify a collision, compute the total kinetic energy before and after. Equal: elastic. Less after: inelastic. Stuck together: perfectly inelastic. In an elastic collision the objects also separate as fast as they approached: $v_2' - v_1' = v_1 - v_2$.

Where does that separation rule come from? Write momentum as $m_1(v_1 - v_1') = m_2(v_2' - v_2)$ and kinetic energy as $m_1(v_1^2 - v_1'^2) = m_2(v_2'^2 - v_2^2)$. Factor the squares: $$m_1(v_1 - v_1')(v_1 + v_1') = m_2(v_2' - v_2)(v_2' + v_2).$$ Divide by the momentum equation and you are left with $v_1 + v_1' = v_2 + v_2'$, which rearranges to "separation speed equals approach speed". For a target at rest this gives $$v_1' = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_1, \qquad v_2' = \frac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v_1.$$

Thinking kinetic energy, like momentum, is always conserved. Momentum is protected by the third law; kinetic energy has no such protection and is usually partly turned into thermal energy and sound. Only use "$K$ before = $K$ after" when a problem says the collision is elastic (or you have checked it). Quick test: if the objects stick, it cannot be elastic.

blocks.html: An explosion is a collision run backward. Pieces that start together at rest fly apart, and conservation of momentum says how their speeds compare.

If a system starts at rest and only internal forces push the pieces apart, the total momentum stays zero: $$m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_2 = -\frac{m_1}{m_2}v_1.$$ The pieces get equal and opposite momenta. The lighter piece moves faster, in proportion to the mass ratio.

The push between the pieces is one third-law pair: equal forces, opposite directions, same time. So the impulses are equal and opposite, and each piece leaves with momentum of the same size. Kinetic energy is not conserved here; it starts at zero. It comes from stored energy: a compressed spring, muscles, or the chemical energy of gunpowder or rocket fuel. Because $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$ and the momenta are equal in size, the lighter piece gets more of that energy.

blocks.html: The center of mass of a system is its mass-weighted average position. It turns out to move in the simplest way possible, and that gives a second view of momentum conservation.

Take two objects. Their center of mass is at $x_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{m_1x_1 + m_2x_2}{m_1 + m_2}$. In a short time each object moves $v\Delta t$, so the center of mass moves with velocity $$v_{\text{cm}} = \frac{m_1v_1 + m_2v_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{p_{\text{tot}}}{M}.$$ If the total momentum is constant, so is $v_{\text{cm}}$. More generally, $\Sigma F_{\text{ext}} = M a_{\text{cm}}$: only outside forces can change how the center of mass moves.

The center of mass moves as if all the mass were there and every outside force acted on it. With no net outside force, it moves in a straight line at constant speed (or stays at rest), no matter how the parts collide, push apart or explode.

blocks.html: Everything you learned about motion along a line has a twin for things that turn: wheels, fans, planets, a door. The turning versions use angles instead of distances, and the angle unit that makes everything work is the radian, which you met with arc length.

A radian measures an angle by the arc it cuts: $\theta = \dfrac{s}{r}$, arc length over radius. A full circle has arc $2\pi r$, so a full turn is $\dfrac{2\pi r}{r} = 2\pi$ rad. Because $\theta$ is a ratio of two lengths, the radian has no real unit, and that is exactly why formulas such as $s = r\theta$ and $v = r\omega$ work with no conversion factor, but only when the angle is in radians.

Angular position $\theta$ in radians ($1\ \text{rev} = 2\pi\ \text{rad} = 360^\circ$). Angular velocity $\omega = \dfrac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}$ in rad/s. Angular acceleration $\alpha = \dfrac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t}$ in rad/s². Counterclockwise is usually positive, and $\alpha$ against the turning means slowing down.

blocks.html: When the angular acceleration is constant, turning follows the same equations as motion with constant acceleration, with each letter swapped for its rotational twin.

The straight-line equations came from two facts: velocity changes at a steady rate, and displacement is the area under the velocity–time graph. Both facts hold for turning. If $\alpha$ is constant, $\omega$ rises along a straight line in time, and the angle turned is the area under the $\omega$–$t$ graph. So the algebra is identical; only the names change.

blocks.html: With constant $\alpha$: $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$, $\Delta\theta = \omega_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$ and $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\Delta\theta$. Angles in radians, $\omega$ in rad/s, $\alpha$ in rad/s². Divide radians by $2\pi$ to count revolutions.

blocks.html: A spinning wheel has one angular velocity, yet its parts move at different speeds. Linking the two kinds of quantity explains why, and it ties turning to centripetal acceleration.

A point at radius $r$ that turns through $\Delta\theta$ travels the arc $\Delta s = r\Delta\theta$. Divide by the time: its speed is $v = \dfrac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} = r\dfrac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t} = r\omega$. If $\omega$ changes, $v$ changes $r$ times as fast: the tangential acceleration is $a_t = r\alpha$. And moving in a circle at speed $v$ always needs the centripetal acceleration $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = r\omega^2$, toward the center.

For a point at distance $r$ from the axis (angles in radians): speed $v = r\omega$, tangential acceleration $a_t = r\alpha$ (along the path), centripetal acceleration $a_c = r\omega^2$ (toward the center). All points share one $\omega$ and $\alpha$, but $v$, $a_t$ and $a_c$ grow with $r$.

blocks.html: A lever balances when force times distance from the pivot is the same on both sides. Torque is the general version of that rule. It measures how strongly a force turns something about an axis, and it depends on more than the size of the force. To find it you will use force components.

Push on a door. Push near the hinges and it barely moves; push at the edge and it swings easily. Push straight toward the hinges and nothing happens, however hard you push. Only the part of the force at right angles to the door, $F_\perp = F\sin\theta$, turns it, and its effect grows with the distance $r$ from the hinge. So the turning effect is $\tau = rF\sin\theta$. You can read the same product another way: $r\sin\theta$ is the lever arm $r_\perp$, the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line along which the force acts.

$$\tau = rF\sin\theta = rF_\perp = r_\perp F,$$ where $r$ is the distance from the axis to where the force acts and $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{F}$. Unit: $\text{N·m}$. Give torques a sign: counterclockwise positive, clockwise negative, and add them for the net torque.

blocks.html: Thinking a bigger force always makes a bigger torque. Torque depends on three things: the force, where it acts and its direction. A $150\ \text{N}$ push straight toward the hinges makes no torque, while $40\ \text{N}$ at the edge, at right angles, turns the door easily. Check each force's lever arm before comparing.
Torque and work share the unit $\text{N·m}$, but they are different things: torque is a turning effect, work is energy. Physicists write work in joules and torque in $\text{N·m}$ to keep them apart.

blocks.html: An object at rest in equilibrium needs zero net force. That is not enough: two equal, opposite forces at the two ends of a ruler cancel, yet the ruler spins. So a second condition joins the first, written with torque.

An object is in static equilibrium when both $\Sigma\vec{F} = 0$ (no acceleration) and $\Sigma\tau = 0$ (no angular acceleration). If the forces add to zero, the net torque is the same about every point, so you may take torques about whatever point is most convenient.

Why can you pick any pivot? Move the reference point a distance $d$ along a beam. Each vertical force's torque changes by $-dF$, so the net torque changes by $-d\,\Sigma F$. When $\Sigma F = 0$, that change is zero. Smart choice: put the pivot where an unknown force acts. Its lever arm is then zero, it drops out of the torque equation, and you can solve for the other unknown at once.

items: Draw every force on the object, including the force at the pivot or support and the object's own weight at its center of mass.
Choose a pivot at an unknown force.
Write $\Sigma\tau = 0$ (counterclockwise positive) and solve.
Use $\Sigma F = 0$ for anything left, and as a check.

steps: Pivot at the hinge, so the unknown hinge force drops out.
The cable's torque is $T(2.0)\sin 30^\circ = 1.0\,T$; the weights give $(98)(1.0) + (196)(2.0) = 490\ \text{N·m}$ the other way.
$T = 490\ \text{N}$, more than the sign's weight, because the cable pulls at a shallow angle.

In equilibrium every pivot gives the same, correct answers; a clever pivot only makes the algebra shorter. But when you switch to a new point, the support force at the old pivot now has a lever arm and must be included. Check: solve once about each support; the two answers must satisfy $\Sigma F = 0$.

blocks.html: Mass tells you how hard it is to change straight-line motion. For turning, what matters is not only how much mass there is, but how far it sits from the axis. That is rotational inertia, built from the torque needed to spin something up and the idea of a system of masses.

Picture one small mass $m$ on a light rod, a distance $r$ from the axis. Push it along its circle with force $F$: $F = ma_t = m(r\alpha)$. The torque of that push is $\tau = rF = mr^2\alpha$. So the "rotational mass" of this one bead is $mr^2$. The same bead twice as far out is four times as hard to spin up: for the same $\alpha$ it needs twice the acceleration, so twice the force, and that force acts at twice the distance, which doubles the torque again. For many pieces, add them up.

Rotational inertia: $I = \Sigma m r^2$, with $r$ measured from the axis, in $\text{kg·m}^2$. Mass far from the axis counts much more than mass near it. For common shapes of mass $M$ and radius $R$: hoop $MR^2$, solid disk or cylinder $\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$, solid sphere $\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$, thin hollow sphere $\tfrac{2}{3}MR^2$, thin rod about its center $\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2$, about one end $\tfrac{1}{3}ML^2$.

opts.task: Drag the beads along the rod. Moving one bead from $0.2\ \text{m}$ to $0.4\ \text{m}$ makes its share of $I$ four times larger.

blocks.cap: Same beads, same mass; only their distance from the axis changes $I$.

blocks.title: Beads on a rod
blocks.q: A light rod spins about its middle. It carries $2.0\ \text{kg}$ at $0.30\ \text{m}$ on one side and $1.0\ \text{kg}$ at $0.50\ \text{m}$ on the other. Find $I$.
steps: The lighter bead contributes more because it is farther out.

blocks.title: Same object, different axis
blocks.q: The same two beads, but now the axis passes through the $2.0\ \text{kg}$ bead, so the other bead is $0.80\ \text{m}$ away. Find $I$.
steps: The bead on the axis has $r = 0$ and adds nothing.
$I = (1.0)(0.80)^2 = 0.64\ \text{kg·m}^2$, larger than before: $I$ depends on the axis.

blocks.title: A disk with a lump
blocks.q: A $4.0\ \text{kg}$ solid disk of radius $0.25\ \text{m}$ has $0.50\ \text{kg}$ of clay stuck to its rim. Find $I$ about its center.
steps: $I = 0.156\ \text{kg·m}^2$. The clay is one ninth of the mass but adds a quarter as much again.

blocks.html: Thinking rotational inertia depends only on the mass. A hoop and a disk of the same mass and radius have different $I$ ($MR^2$ against $\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$), because the hoop keeps all its mass at the rim. Moving mass outward raises $I$ even though the mass doesn't change. Check: every term in $I$ has $r^2$ in it; if your answer doesn't use distances from the axis, it can't be right.

blocks.html: Newton's second law says a net force gives a mass an acceleration. The rotational version swaps each piece for its twin: net torque, rotational inertia and angular acceleration.

For one bead of mass $m$ at radius $r$, a push along its circle gives $\tau = mr^2\alpha$. A rigid object is many beads that all share the same $\alpha$, so the torques add: $\Sigma\tau = (\Sigma mr^2)\alpha = I\alpha$. The forces the beads exert on each other come in third-law pairs along the lines between them, and their torques cancel, so only outside torques remain.

$$\Sigma\tau = I\alpha.$$ The net torque about an axis equals the rotational inertia about that axis times the angular acceleration. Torque plays the role of force and $I$ plays the role of mass. Use signs: counterclockwise positive.

blocks.name: ph-rotation
blocks.cap: A falling mass pulls a cord wrapped around a heavy disk. The cord's tension gives the torque $TR$, and the disk's $I = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$ sets how quickly it spins up.

blocks.title: A pulled string
blocks.q: A string wrapped around a $5.0\ \text{kg}$ solid disk of radius $0.20\ \text{m}$ is pulled with $10\ \text{N}$. The disk turns on a fixed, frictionless axle. Find $\alpha$.
steps: Torque: the string pulls along the rim, so $\tau = RF = (0.20)(10) = 2.0\ \text{N·m}$.

blocks.title: Braking a wheel
blocks.q: A wheel with $I = 1.2\ \text{kg·m}^2$ turns at $120$ rpm. A brake stops it in $6.0\ \text{s}$. What steady torque does the brake apply?

blocks.title: Two ropes, opposite ways
blocks.q: A wheel ($I = 0.10\ \text{kg·m}^2$) has a rope at radius $0.10\ \text{m}$ pulling $20\ \text{N}$ counterclockwise and one at $0.25\ \text{m}$ pulling $10\ \text{N}$ clockwise. Find $\alpha$.
steps: $\alpha = \dfrac{-0.5}{0.10} = -5.0\ \text{rad/s}^2$: clockwise, though the counterclockwise rope pulls twice as hard.

blocks.html: Using the force instead of the torque, or the mass instead of the rotational inertia. Writing $\alpha = F/m$ gives units of $\text{m/s}^2$, not $\text{rad/s}^2$: a sign the formula doesn't fit. In rotation, every force enters through its torque ($rF\sin\theta$), and every mass through $I$. Check the units: $\text{N·m} \div \text{kg·m}^2 = \text{1/s}^2$, which is rad/s².

blocks.html: In pulley problems so far, the pulley was light, so one tension ran all the way around it. A real pulley has mass and has to be spun up, which takes a net torque. This topic joins $\Sigma\tau = I\alpha$ to $\Sigma F = ma$, using $a = R\alpha$.

For the pulley to gain angular velocity, the torques on it can't cancel: $(T_2 - T_1)R = I\alpha$. So the tension on the side that is pulled harder must be larger. Only if $I = 0$ do the two tensions match. A cord that doesn't slip ties the motions together: the cord, the hanging masses and the pulley's rim all move with the same $a$, and $a = R\alpha$.

Write one equation for each object: $\Sigma F = ma$ for each hanging mass, $\Sigma\tau = I\alpha$ for the pulley, and link them with $a = R\alpha$. For a uniform disk pulley ($I = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$), the pulley acts like an extra mass $\tfrac{1}{2}M$ that must be accelerated, and $R$ cancels.

blocks.cap: An Atwood machine with a heavy pulley. $T_2 > T_1$: the difference is what spins the pulley up.

blocks.html: Assuming the tension is the same on both sides of a pulley that has mass. Equal tensions would give zero net torque, and the pulley could never start turning. Use two different tensions and let the pulley's equation decide their difference. Check: with $M = 0$ your answers should turn into the light-pulley results, and with $M > 0$ the acceleration must come out smaller.

blocks.html: A flywheel spinning in place goes nowhere, yet it can light a bulb or lift a weight: it stores kinetic energy. This topic finds how much, using rotational inertia, and extends the work-energy theorem to turning.

Split a spinning object into small pieces. A piece of mass $m$ at radius $r$ moves at $v = r\omega$, so its kinetic energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}m(r\omega)^2$. Every piece shares the same $\omega$, so adding them gives $$K = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\Sigma mr^2\right)\omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2.$$ For work: a force $F$ at radius $r$ pushing a piece along an arc $s = r\Delta\theta$ does work $Fs = (rF)\Delta\theta = \tau\Delta\theta$.

A spinning object stores $K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ ($\omega$ in rad/s). A torque turning it through $\Delta\theta$ (in radians) does work $W = \tau\Delta\theta$, and the net work equals the change in rotational kinetic energy: $\Sigma\tau\,\Delta\theta = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega_f^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega_i^2$.

blocks.name: ph-rotation

opts.task: Compare the dots: the rim dot moves four times as fast as the inner one, so each kilogram there carries sixteen times the kinetic energy.

blocks.cap: Speeds grow with radius ($v = r\omega$), so kinetic energy is concentrated near the rim. That is why flywheels put their mass in a heavy outer ring.

blocks.title: A spinning flywheel
blocks.q: A solid-disk flywheel ($50\ \text{kg}$, radius $0.30\ \text{m}$) spins at $600$ rpm. How much kinetic energy does it store?
steps: $K = \tfrac{1}{2}(2.25)(62.8)^2 = 4440\ \text{J}$, about the energy needed to lift a $45\ \text{kg}$ person $10\ \text{m}$.

blocks.title: Spinning up with a torque
blocks.q: A motor applies a net torque of $4.0\ \text{N·m}$ to a wheel ($I = 0.50\ \text{kg·m}^2$) at rest while it turns $5$ revolutions. Find its final $\omega$.

blocks.html: Using $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ with the rim speed for an object that only spins. Only the rim moves at that speed; everything inside moves more slowly. For a solid disk, $\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2\right)\left(\tfrac{v}{R}\right)^2 = \tfrac{1}{4}Mv^2$, half of $\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2$. Another trap is $\omega$ in rpm: $\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ needs rad/s. Check: a spinning object's $K$ can never be more than $\tfrac{1}{2}Mv_{\text{rim}}^2$, which only a thin hoop reaches.
Rotational kinetic energy is the second kind of kinetic energy. An object can have both: a rolling ball moves and spins at once, which is the next topic.

blocks.html: A rolling ball does two things at once: its center moves, and it spins. So it has two kinds of kinetic energy, the ordinary kind and rotational kinetic energy. Adding both to energy conservation explains a famous race.

Rolling without slipping means the point touching the ground is momentarily at rest, like the bottom of a tire tread. The center then moves the distance $R\Delta\theta$ while the object turns $\Delta\theta$, so $v = R\omega$. With $I = cmR^2$ (where $c$ depends on the shape), the total kinetic energy is $$K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}(cmR^2)\left(\frac{v}{R}\right)^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + c)\,mv^2.$$ Static friction at the contact point does no work, because that point doesn't slide, so mechanical energy is conserved down a ramp: $mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + c)mv^2$.

For rolling without slipping: $v = R\omega$ and $K = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + c)mv^2$, with $c = \dfrac{I}{mR^2}$: hoop $1$, hollow sphere $\tfrac{2}{3}$, solid cylinder $\tfrac{1}{2}$, solid sphere $\tfrac{2}{5}$. From rest down a height $h$: $$v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1 + c}}.$$ Mass and radius cancel; only the shape matters.

opts.task: Press Play. Then change the ramp angle: the finishing order never changes.

blocks.cap: The race: solid sphere first, then the solid disk (a cylinder), the hollow sphere, and the hoop last. The less a shape spends on spinning, the faster it moves.

blocks.title: Kinetic energy of a rolling can
blocks.q: A $2.0\ \text{kg}$ solid cylinder rolls at $3.0\ \text{m/s}$. Find its total kinetic energy.
steps: Total: $13.5\ \text{J}$. One third of it is spinning energy.

blocks.title: Speed at the bottom
blocks.q: A solid ball rolls from rest down a ramp, dropping $1.4\ \text{m}$. How fast is it moving at the bottom?
steps: A frictionless sliding block would reach $\sqrt{2(9.8)(1.4)} = 5.2\ \text{m/s}$. The ball is slower because $\tfrac{2}{7}$ of its energy goes into spinning.

blocks.title: Rolling uphill
blocks.q: A hoop rolls toward a hill at $2.0\ \text{m/s}$. How high does it roll before stopping?
steps: All its kinetic energy becomes potential energy: $\tfrac{1}{2}(1 + 1)mv^2 = mgh$.
$h = \dfrac{2v^2}{2g} = \dfrac{(2.0)^2}{9.8} = 0.41\ \text{m}$, twice as high as a sliding block with the same speed would go.

blocks.html: Thinking the heavier or larger ball wins a rolling race. In $v = \sqrt{2gh/(1 + c)}$ there is no $m$ and no $R$. A heavy solid ball and a light solid ball tie; a solid ball beats a hoop of any size. Check: if your answer for a rolling speed depends on the mass, a step has gone wrong (or something other than gravity is doing work).

The ramp's static friction is what makes the object spin, yet it takes no energy away: it only shares the energy between moving and spinning. A ball that skids, like a bowling ball just after release, does lose energy to kinetic friction until it starts to roll.

blocks.html: Momentum $p = mv$ measures how hard straight-line motion is to stop. Angular momentum does the same for turning, and the rotational second law gives it in the same way that $F\Delta t = \Delta p$ came from $F = ma$.

Start from $\Sigma\tau = I\alpha = I\dfrac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t}$ and multiply by $\Delta t$: $\Sigma\tau\,\Delta t = \Delta(I\omega)$. The quantity $L = I\omega$ is the angular momentum, and torque times time, the angular impulse, changes it. A single small mass going around a circle of radius $r$ has $I = mr^2$ and $\omega = v/r$, so $L = mr^2\cdot\dfrac{v}{r} = mvr$. That last form works even for a mass moving in a straight line, measured about any point: use $L = mvr_\perp$, where $r_\perp$ is the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of motion.

Angular momentum: $L = I\omega$ for a spinning object, and $L = mvr_\perp$ for a point mass about a chosen point ($r_\perp$ = perpendicular distance from the point to its line of motion). Unit: $\text{kg·m}^2\text{/s}$. Angular impulse changes it: $\tau\,\Delta t = \Delta L$.

blocks.name: phys1-sweep

opts.task: Watch the puck slide past P. The distance $r$ and the angle keep changing, but $r_\perp$ and $L = mvr_\perp$ stay the same, and every shaded triangle has the same area.

blocks.cap: A puck moving in a straight line has angular momentum about P. The line from P sweeps out equal areas in equal times, just as a planet does.

blocks.title: A spinning wheel
blocks.q: A wheel with $I = 0.40\ \text{kg·m}^2$ spins at $15\ \text{rad/s}$. Find its angular momentum.

blocks.title: A skater passing a post
blocks.q: A $60\ \text{kg}$ skater glides in a straight line at $4.0\ \text{m/s}$, passing $1.5\ \text{m}$ from a post at the closest point. Find her angular momentum about the post.
steps: The perpendicular distance from the post to her path is $r_\perp = 1.5\ \text{m}$.
$$L = mvr_\perp = (60)(4.0)(1.5) = 360\ \text{kg·m}^2\text{/s},$$ the same at every point along her path.
If she grabbed a rope tied to the post, she would swing around it with exactly this angular momentum.

blocks.title: Angular impulse
blocks.q: A steady torque of $2.0\ \text{N·m}$ acts for $3.0\ \text{s}$ on a wheel ($I = 0.25\ \text{kg·m}^2$) that starts at rest. Find its final $\omega$.

blocks.html: Thinking an object moving in a straight line can't have angular momentum. Angular momentum is measured about a point. About any point that isn't on its path, a moving object has $L = mvr_\perp$, even though nothing spins. It is zero only about points on the line itself. Check: a puck aimed straight at the post has $r_\perp = 0$, and one passing to the side does not.

blocks.html: An angular impulse $\tau\Delta t$ changes angular momentum. So when no outside torque acts, angular momentum cannot change at all, which explains spinning skaters, divers, and why planets speed up near the Sun.

If the net outside torque on a system is zero, its angular momentum stays the same: $$I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2.$$ Pull mass toward the axis (smaller $I$) and the spin speeds up; push it outward and the spin slows.

Inside a system, every force has a third-law partner, equal, opposite and along the same line, so their torques cancel. Only outside torques can change the total $L$. A skater on smooth ice feels almost no torque about her vertical axis, so her $L$ is fixed. Her kinetic energy is not: writing $K = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \dfrac{L^2}{2I}$, the same $L$ with a smaller $I$ means a bigger $K$. The extra energy comes from the work her arms do pulling the weights inward, against their tendency to keep moving in a straight line.

opts.task: Slide the arms in. $L$ (teal) stays put while $\omega$ and $K$ grow.

steps: Friction between them is internal: $I_1\omega_1 = (I_1 + I_2)\omega_f$.
Like a sticking collision: angular momentum is kept, but kinetic energy drops (to two thirds here).

Conservation of one quantity doesn't mean conservation of the other, just as momentum but not kinetic energy survives a sticking collision. blocks.html: A satellite circles Earth because gravity pulls it toward the center while it moves sideways. Gravity is the centripetal force. That one idea gives the orbital speed, the period, and why the people inside float.

Imagine Newton's cannon on a very tall mountain. Fire a ball sideways and it curves down to the ground. Fire it faster and it lands farther away. At about $7.9\ \text{km/s}$ near Earth's surface, the ground curves away as fast as the ball falls: it keeps falling and never lands. That is an orbit. For a circle of radius $r$ (measured from the planet's center), gravity must supply exactly the centripetal force: $$\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}.$$ The satellite's own mass cancels.

For a circular orbit of radius $r = R + h$ around a planet of mass $M$: $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$ and period $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v}$. Lower orbits are faster, and take less time. Everything in an orbiting craft falls together, so it feels weightless even though gravity is strong.

steps: Gravity points at Earth's center, so it makes no torque about it, and angular momentum is conserved.
At both ends the velocity is perpendicular to the radius: $v_p r_p = v_a r_a$.
$v_a = (9.0\ \text{km/s})\dfrac{7.0 \times 10^{6}}{2.1 \times 10^{7}} = 3.0\ \text{km/s}$: slowest when farthest, which is Kepler's second law.

blocks.cap: Equal areas in equal times: the line from the Sun sweeps out the same area each month, so the planet moves fastest when it is closest. This is angular momentum conservation.

blocks.html: Thinking astronauts float because there is no gravity in orbit. At $400\ \text{km}$ up, gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground, and it is the very force that keeps the station on its curved path. Without it the station would fly off in a straight line. The astronauts float because they are in free fall along with their ship: nothing has to hold them up, just as you feel light at the top of a drop ride.

Higher orbits are slower and take longer: a satellite about $35{,}800\ \text{km}$ up takes one day to go around, so it stays above one spot on the equator. Fly your own orbits in the Orbit Lab of the Science Lab.

blocks.html: Pull a mass on a spring and let go: it swings back and forth, again and again. A swing, a guitar string and a building in an earthquake do the same. You already know how to describe a repeating motion by its amplitude, period and frequency; this topic explains what makes the motion repeat.

The spring force is a restoring force: it always points back toward equilibrium, and it grows in proportion to the displacement, $F = -kx$. So the acceleration is $$a = \frac{F}{m} = -\frac{k}{m}x.$$ Released at $x = A$, the mass is pulled back and speeds up. At $x = 0$ the force vanishes, but the mass is moving fast and overshoots. Now the spring pulls the other way, slows it, and stops it at $x = -A$. Then the whole thing runs in reverse. With no friction, nothing is lost, so it repeats forever between $+A$ and $-A$. Motion driven by a force like this is called simple harmonic motion (SHM).

Simple harmonic motion comes from a restoring force proportional to displacement, $F = -kx$, so $a = -\dfrac{k}{m}x$. The amplitude $A$ is the largest displacement; the period $T$ is the time for one full cycle; the frequency is $f = \dfrac{1}{T}$, in hertz (cycles per second).

steps: $$a = -\dfrac{k}{m}x = -\dfrac{80}{0.50}(-0.05) = +8.0\ \text{m/s}^2:$$ to the right, back toward the middle.

blocks.title: Distance in a few cycles
blocks.q: An oscillator with amplitude $0.10\ \text{m}$ runs for $3$ full periods. How far does it travel?
steps: One cycle: from $+A$ to $-A$ and back, a distance of $4A = 0.40\ \text{m}$.
Three cycles: $1.2\ \text{m}$, though it ends exactly where it started (zero displacement).

blocks.html: Thinking the acceleration is greatest at the middle, where the speed is greatest. The acceleration depends on the position, $a = -\tfrac{k}{m}x$, not on the speed. At the middle $x = 0$, so the force and acceleration are zero; at the turning points the mass is momentarily at rest, yet its acceleration is largest. Check with the graphs above: the $a$ curve is zero exactly when the $x$ curve crosses zero.

blocks.html: What sets how fast a simple harmonic oscillator repeats? A heavier mass should be more sluggish, and a stiffer spring should snap it back faster. The exact rule involves a square root, and a link to circular motion shows where it comes from.

Picture a point going around a circle of radius $A$ at steady angular speed $\omega$. Its shadow on the $x$-axis moves back and forth between $+A$ and $-A$. The point's centripetal acceleration is $A\omega^2$ toward the center, and its $x$-part is $-\omega^2 x$: the shadow's acceleration is proportional to its displacement and opposite to it, exactly like SHM. A spring gives $a = -\dfrac{k}{m}x$, so the spring's motion matches a shadow with $\omega^2 = \dfrac{k}{m}$. One trip around the circle takes $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$, so $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}.$$

A mass $m$ on a spring of constant $k$ oscillates with period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$ and frequency $f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}$. The amplitude does not appear: big and small swings take the same time. Four times the mass doubles the period.

blocks.q: A mass stretches a vertical spring $2.5\ \text{cm}$ when it hangs at rest. Find the period when it bobs.
steps: At rest, $k\Delta x = mg$, so $\dfrac{m}{k} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{g}$.
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{0.025\ \text{m}}{9.8\ \text{m/s}^2}} = 0.32\ \text{s}$. Gravity shifts where the middle is, not how long a cycle takes.

blocks.html: Thinking a bigger amplitude makes the period longer. A longer trip seems to need more time, but a bigger stretch also means a bigger force and higher speeds, and the two effects cancel exactly: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ has no $A$ in it. Check: pull a spring toy twice as far and count the bounces in ten seconds; the count doesn't change. This is why springs and pendulums make good clocks.

blocks.html: A pendulum has no spring, yet it swings in nearly perfect simple harmonic motion. Gravity, the same pull that makes things fall, provides the restoring force.

Pull the bob aside by an angle $\theta$. Gravity $mg$ splits into a part along the string (balanced by the tension) and a part along the arc, $mg\sin\theta$, back toward the bottom. For small angles, $\sin\theta \approx \theta = \dfrac{x}{L}$, where $x$ is the distance along the arc. So the restoring force is about $$F = -\frac{mg}{L}x,$$ the same form as a spring with "$k$" $= \dfrac{mg}{L}$. Put that into $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{mg/L}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}.$$ The mass cancels: a heavier bob is pulled harder but is harder to speed up, in the same proportion.

For small swings, a simple pendulum of length $L$ (pivot to the center of the bob) has period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$. It depends on the length and on $g$ only, not on the mass or (for small angles) the amplitude. Four times the length doubles the period.

blocks.html: Thinking a heavier bob swings more slowly. A heavier bob does feel a bigger restoring pull, but it has more inertia in exactly the same proportion, so its motion is unchanged: there is no $m$ in $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$. To slow a pendulum, make it longer. Check: in the visual above, the heavy and light bobs stay in step.

"Small" swings means up to about $15^\circ$: there the formula is off by less than half a percent. Big swings take a little longer, because $\sin\theta$ grows more slowly than $\theta$. You can see this in the Pendulums and Resonance lab of the Science Lab.

blocks.html: An oscillator trades energy back and forth between motion and storage. Conservation of mechanical energy turns that trade into quick answers about speeds, without any graphs or timing, for any simple harmonic oscillator.

A spring stretched by $x$ stores $U = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$. With no friction, the total $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$ never changes. At a turning point the mass stops for an instant, so all the energy is stored: $E = \tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$. At equilibrium the spring stores nothing, so all of it is kinetic: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}kA^2$. In between, the energy is shared.

$$\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}kA^2.$$ The speed is greatest at equilibrium, $v_{\max} = A\sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}$, and zero at the turning points. At any position, $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}\left(A^2 - x^2\right)}$.

blocks.html: The reference circle gave the period of simple harmonic motion. It also gives the whole motion as a graph, and you can read velocity and acceleration from it just as you did with motion graphs along a line.

Follow a point around a circle of radius $A$ at angular speed $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$, starting at $x = A$. Its shadow is at $x = A\cos(\omega t)$. The point's velocity has size $A\omega$ along the circle, and the shadow gets the $x$-part of it: $v = -A\omega\sin(\omega t)$. Its acceleration has size $A\omega^2$ toward the center, and the shadow's part is $a = -A\omega^2\cos(\omega t) = -\omega^2 x$. Cosine and sine are the same wave shifted by a quarter turn, so the three graphs are a quarter cycle apart.

Starting from $x = A$ at rest: $$x = A\cos\frac{2\pi t}{T}, \quad v = -\frac{2\pi A}{T}\sin\frac{2\pi t}{T}, \quad a = -\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2 x.$$ The greatest speed is $v_{\max} = \dfrac{2\pi A}{T}$ and the greatest acceleration is $a_{\max} = \left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2 A$. Velocity peaks a quarter cycle after position; acceleration is always opposite to position.
